title: Babies Prefer the Helper
text:
In 2007 Kiley Hamlin, Karen Wynn and Paul Bloom of Yale University asked whether babies who cannot yet talk already judge others by how they treat people.

They showed six- and ten-month-old infants a little puppet show. A wooden toy with large googly eyes, the climber, tried again and again to get up a steep hill. On some attempts, another toy came from below and pushed it up to the top: the helper. On others, a different toy came from above and pushed it back down: the hinderer. The helper and hinderer differed in color and shape, and these were swapped across babies.

Afterward, a researcher who did not know which toy had played which role held both out to the baby. In the original study, almost all the infants reached for the helper, 14 of 16 ten-month-olds and all 12 six-month-olds. Further experiments suggested that babies preferred a helper to a neutral toy, and a neutral toy to a hinderer. The researchers argued that the ability to evaluate others by their actions toward third parties appears very early in life, before language, and may be a foundation of later moral judgment.
lesson: How we treat others is noticed, possibly from our earliest months. People judge us by what we do to those around us, not just by what we do to them.
people: Kiley Hamlin, Karen Wynn, Paul Bloom
source: Hamlin, J. K., Wynn, K., and Bloom, P. (2007). Social evaluation by preverbal infants. Nature, 450, 557-559.
caveat: Replications have been mixed, and a large multi-lab replication did not find a clear preference for the helper.
